Can't blame them when you see how they're treated. - Reliance on consulting firms to "help" with business decisions. - The Atrium building in Buffalo is by far the worst office I've ever worked in. No personal space, noisy environment, sub-par canteen with very limited outside options, undersized restrooms, surveillance cameras in the actual work area... headline: Administrator
pros: I've been working here for 10+yrs. I came into the business with no knowledge of the Optics industry, so everything I have learned has come from Specsavers. They seem keen to allow people who have no previous experience to join the team., and invest in training and education. Job security, I know that I won't just be cut loose, I've never known anyone to be made redundant in the time I've been there. Company attitude to value and quality of service and products is laudable but is let down by individuals within the team. It's very easy to turn up, do my job and leave at the end of each day.
cons: There are so many levels of inequality. Only team members SEEN to be making money for the business are rewarded with any kind of bonus. None of the supporting staff is considered valuable and there is a culture of not following tasks through to completion and assuming that the support staff are happy to pick up the loose ends. I myself spend 40-50% of my working week tying up unfinished or sloppy work, some of those staff can be paid 5x what I am!! People who have been there a long time and who have made no effort to establish a high standard of work are simply allowed to continue with their sloppy attitudes but if you raise your own standards at any time you are punished for not meeting those standards regularly, so those who don't bother are simply allowed or encouraged to coast through. This has led to different standards/rules being applied to different people. The culture among the employees is very clicky, you have to be a confident strong personality to survive, let alone win any popularity contest, only popular staff get a collection at their birthdays or when going on maternity leave or leaving the company. I have never had a birthday whip round. Customers get a better deal on discounted products than staff!! Communication of information to the staff is appalling. At this time the opening hours are changing in less than a month and we haven't been officially told, I found out by pure mistake. You don't really know who is senior and who isn't, and there are far too many members of the management team! We are required to give 6 weeks notice for booking time off (fair enough) but we have to attend meetings out of hours with 2 weeks notice. Yet another example of double standards. Nothing ever changes. When failures in processes are identified, they are looked at and changed for a few weeks then old habits come back! It's pot luck whether you get to someone in IT who knows what they are doing. We know very little about the CEO so I can't comment on him.

headline: WORST PLACE TO WORK, THINK TWICE BEFORE GETTING A JOB HERE!!
pros: The benefits such as half price current account, share match, salary and pension!
cons: There is not a single nice thing I can say about Lloyds, just think very carefully before working here. Its a bullying culture and the managers dont care about their staff at all. They put huge amounts of pressure to sell, even though no targets. They expect you to work overtime for free, and in a lot of cases not getting out until 6.30pm but only paid until 5pm. They support mental health, yet make staff suffer in silence. Too many middle managers that want to recieve big bonus`s! They expect you to turn up at 8.30 am and be ready for a meeting at 8.45am, however not paid until 9am. If you turn up after 8.45am they`ll leave you on the doorstep as punishment. Service calls are a nightmare- if you dont get a good one then there is a huge witch hunt from middle managers to find out who is to blame for not getting top scores, making staff scared to death to get a service call. sadly, all the bad practices from 12 years ago are coming back and I fear it will be another slap on the hand from the FCA and maybe more fines coming the banks way. I would not hesitate to say- do not work for lloyds if you value your sanity, work life balance and dignity... they`ll rip it all from you!!

Masses of work outsourced and makes it unfathomable to work through processes, if any exist at all. The C&W business still operates as a separate business and no sign of any organisational or cultural integration.

headline: Marketing

cons: Written by a millennial: Currently, IBM is going through a massive change where everyone has to relocate to one of 6 cities. This tactic is to get rid of the middle/higher level positions who are older & cost more for employment & targeting millennials to hire in. This tactic disregards the expertise that the mid-higher level employees have in their field. Team members who have been at IBM for 20+ years are unappreciated & forced into retirement or to look for a new job. In addition to IBM not appreciating their loyal & experienced employees, IBM has a horrible onboarding process. Starting as a university hire, I was just dropped in without understanding my role, the dynamics of the team, & was assigned as the lead for large events within the first couple months. If IBM plans to replace all of the experienced IBM employees with new young hires, they need to have a very thorough training process in plan based on roles that has a single person assigned to the success of the new hire. Lastly, all direction comes from the top down. Reorganization happens at least once a year if not more. The majority of the time people are trying to understand their role & new team members instead of being able to get quality work done.

headline: Expect to be treat like a slave

Could've been resolved in 1-2 days. - Do not arrive back to your desk 0.001 seconds late for anything. You will be asked to go to a probation review. That's not a joke!

headline: Stable job
pros: They will give you a permanent contract from the beginning, with a 3 month probation time. If your contract says 20 hours per week, you will never work less than that, unless you call in sick. Shifts are fixed, which means you'll always have the same schedule, so you know how to plan the rest of the day. Depending on the floor and department you're working for, there is a pretty good chance you can get overtime hours too. And if the managers see that you're hardworking and eager to get more hours, they won't hesitate to call you when they'll need someone. Tasks vary from day to day, even from hour to hour sometimes, which can be good, it keeps you moving, never getting too bored. Managers are ok. They are usually nice people, understanding, easy to talk to.
cons: AC is never on point. During summer, temperatures can go pretty high inside the store. And because you have to move all the time, tidying and attending to customers, maybe even serve at the tills, you'll obviously going to feel even warmer. And the uniforms don't help with that either, as they're only 33% cotton, which means you're going to sweat and you're not aloud to have any water on the shop floor! During winters, it can get pretty cold. But if you learn to move fast enough and have a fleece with you just in case, you're ok. Be ready to have all different kinds of customers, all in one day. They will not care how tidy your piles look or how neatly you've hanged the items, everything can end up on the floor in a matter of seconds. There are no benefits or discounts for employees, except for 2 weeks in December, which I believe is not fair, considering we're being paid minimum wage. Don't even consider applying for anything else within the company before you get one full year of experience with them on your current position. They won't let you change absolutely anything: you won't be able to ask for a different shift, try to apply for a promotion or a vacancy in a different department without a recommendation from your floor manager.

Tasks vary from day to day, even from hour to hour sometimes, which can be good, it keeps you moving, never getting too bored. Managers are ok. They are usually nice people, understanding, easy to talk to. AC is never on point. During summer, temperatures can go pretty high inside the store. And because you have to move all the time, tidying and attending to customers, maybe even serve at the tills, you'll obviously going to feel even warmer. And the uniforms don't help with that either, as they're only 33% cotton, which means you're going to sweat and you're not aloud to have any water on the shop floor! During winters, it can get pretty cold. But if you learn to move fast enough and have a fleece with you just in case, you're ok. Be ready to have all different kinds of customers, all in one day. They will not care how tidy your piles look or how neatly you've hanged the items, everything can end up on the floor in a matter of seconds. There are no benefits or discounts for employees, except for 2 weeks in December, which I believe is not fair, considering we're being paid minimum wage. Don't even consider applying for anything else within the company before you get one full year of experience with them on your current position. They won't let you change absolutely anything: you won't be able to ask for a different shift, try to apply for a promotion or a vacancy in a different department without a recommendation from your floor manager.

headline: Former Blue Harmony Team Lead
pros: The greatest thing about IBM is their work/life balance, the benefits, the Teams I worked with and the Leadership of the Managers and Team Leads that I worked under. The best in the business! IBM was my dream job a long time before I was hired FT. Before being hired FT with a once then reputable company, I was a contractor. The IBM Management that I reported to saw my worth and treated me and others with respect. When I was hired, it was a dream come true. All my hard work finally paid off. I worked with phenominal people who were patient, and compassionate with their peers and IBM. At that time, IBM was doing quite well. Life was great for all until 9/11/2001 happened. Todays IBM may be different. It may be growing in a more positive direction.
cons: When 9/11/2001 happened, it took a toll on IBM as well as other businesses. The 9/11 affect was a slow trickle of poison to IBMs business. However, I loved my job and the area I worked. I thrived along with my peers. Things were great until more and more resource actions were happening. I was fortunate to be where I was until I decided to accept a job offer with no raise but a lateral move where the wind was blowing. In the first year in this job, I worked the hardest I ever had in a job in my entire working life. However, because I was at the bottom end of the totem pole I received an 'average' rating and NO raise. My heartdropped and so did my morale. I had two counterparts doing basically the same thing, and getting paid significantly more, but they were secure and up on the totem pole farther. I knew then that I had two more years to go of being resourced. That was the word in the hallways and it proved to be true. Very disappointing in a company that I had dreamt of working for, for many years. Before that, I excelled and received above average ratings and raises. The fear of being resourced always lingered every time that dreaded news surfaced. To me and others, this was just a way of resourcing employees. Offer someone a new opportunity just so they can give you the shaft. It did not matter how hard you worked. It all depended on your placement on the totem pole. So if you have been working in a job for a while, stay where you are at. Do not leave. I have applied for jobs at IBM since then, that I was very qualified for, but I am not given a fair chance. I even had interviewed for a job before I was kicked out, which I was positive I had, but the response I got was, 'We cannot hire you at this time'. More disappointing news. I believe I am flagged from being given an equal opportumity on jobs that I know I meet the qualifications.

headline: Arrogant culture, no collaboration, bullying management and not an equal opportunity employer
pros: Good benefits, even though health care is becoming expensive. Amazing talks at Microsoft Research, mainly by invited guests. Huge company so there is the possibility to change roles quite easily. The pay is quite good especially because the main location is in WA. Great bus that brings you all over campus. Some new cool Microsoft devices.
cons: My main criticism is that it is not a company that values women in the workplace. I have not observed women getting promoted and women from technical fields are rarely being hired. Teams remain disproportionately male even compared to recent statistics from Google and other competitors. Little effort is made to proactively recruit women in technical positions. Managers from my division regularly and openly discredit women. They bully them (from my personal experience). It feels like Anchorman over there. The maternity/parental benefits are BS. I took them and it cost me a poor review (I was doing great before and in all prior reviews). If you are in my situation, know that a lot of tech companies are proactively hiring women, publishing their statistics as cause for change, and rewarding women for their good technical work. The underlying belief in other companies is that women have equal capacity to be technical and do technical work. This is not the case at Microsoft. Credit is frequently given to male co-workers on the basis of their arrogance and posture. The presumption is that technical contributions in collaborations come from men. This is promoted by managers at many levels. For instance, women are frequently required to justify more of the technical claims on patents then their male counterparts on similar patents. The presumed inequality is part of everyday engagements. Real equal opportunity teams may exist in the company. Just be sure to interview your future Microsoft colleagues and understand the culture you are going into. I have excellent offers in other places now, and I am taking the one that best fits my personality and values. I know I will have a great impact there. I just wished I had moved out sooner from an environment that was toxic for my health. There is no collaboration possible, and unless you are a very vocal person and snarky to a fault, more arrogant people steal the credit for your work. I have struggled with this lack of collaboration and very competitive atmosphere. I was hoping that with the Nokia integration, a more collaborative culture would influence Microsoft leaders, but unfortunately it did not happen and all of those guys got fired anyway. Regarding the interview process, the recruiter really tries to lowball you compared to other companies. This was my experience interviewing initially and then later interviewing internally. Crap tactics like acting baffled and surprised at basic packages offered by many of their competitor companies are the norm. Can they understand more collaborative techniques and work together on a good package? They do not reward PhDs. They do not reward the caliber of the institution you're coming from. It is because most of the management lack graduate education and believe education is useless (I heard it many times at work). A minor thing, no free food, and food becomes quite expensive if you have only 20minutes to eat and need to eat in the local expensive cafeteria in the Commons (about 10-15$ a lunch). Something to budget. The culture is really engraved in every manager who has been there from the start. Of course, you can find an excellent team (it does exist!) and if the work is a good fit, go for it. Be sure to probe the team's culture and get to know who will be your skip level.

cons: So large that the goals of different parts of the company often conflict. Benefits, vacation, pension, stock purchase plan, medical, etc. have all been squeezed in recent years so the fringe benefits of working for IBM are not so great. They're also working hard to transfer jobs out of the USA to China and India, this makes one's future with the company in the USA less stable. The level of expertise of the technical talent can vary widely, many parts of the company are not attractive to really talented people who can get jobs elsewhere.

headline: McDonald's is an ok place to work if you don't mind working long hours and are good at sucking up to your boss.
pros: McDonald's is one of the few companies that is doing well in this weak economy. The strong brand is a huge advantage for the company. For those willing to work long hours, work exceptionally hard and be very agreeable with management, there are advancement opportunities. Benefits are good. The Oak Brook offices are comfortable and well maintained.
cons: McDonald's is very ingrown and not very open to ideas from outsiders. McDonald's values "nice" people over competent people. It's extremely important to not "rock the boat" - management at all levels is not open to suggestions. Success at McDonald's requires a lot of networking and office politics are very important. This isn't a bad thing, it's just something to be aware of. Knowing how the office game is played is important at every company but is especially important at McDonald's. There's a certain type of person who succeeds at McDonald's - very cheerful, kind of bland, willing to work long hours without complaining, able to be extremely tactful. Again, not all bad, just the way it is. I think it's telling that year after year, most departments score low on the employee survey area asking whether "a free exchange of ideas is encouraged." Many managers are of the mindset of "don't tell me any bad news." The other thing to remember about McDonald's is that it's a very large company. There are small pockets of the company that do interesting and innovative work. The Romeoville Innovation Center is a great place to work. It doesn't seem to have the "play it safe" attitude that pervades much of McDonald's. Overall, the company is not bad but in most of the office jobs, it's much more important to get along with people than to be innovative. Ideally, you want people who are both fun to work with and are great at their jobs and it's important that a company inspire a feeling of respect for all employees. McDonald's does try to do this. However, the social and networking aspects of the company and the need to "go along" are so important to an individual's success that someone who is at all outspoken will have a very difficult time here. Everything I've said to this point has to do with professional jobs at McDonald's. Restaurant jobs are boring and poorly paid. Restaurant managers work extremely hard. In many ways, the success of McDonald's is built on the backs of poorly paid overworked restaurant managers and crew.

These managers have often been there a long time and have friends where it matters. Health and safety paranoia gives excuse to punish anyone 'troublesome'. Infantile culture results. Leaving is a great liberation, unless you are a jobsworth perhaps.

headline: My boss is cool. Most aren't.
pros: Working for Apple can be something you take pride in - I write software that my whole family (and millions of other people) get to see and use every day. My work is usually interesting, and I'm mostly surrounded by very smart people. My manager is not typical - he is respectful of my life outside of work. My work schedule is very flexible thanks to that. I'm always able to take vacations, and I'm able to telecommute once a week, sometimes twice if I need to. I haven't come into the office on the weekend at all during the last 4-5 years. Since 2007-2008, our cafeteria is awesome. It really sucked before that. The burrito bar kicks ass now. Cafeteria food costs $$$ - it's not free.
cons: Many departments, and their VP's, directors, and managers have unrealistic expectations of their employees. Particularly on the hardware engineering side of Infinite Loop (buildings 5 and 6), people get driven very hard and are regularly expected to work weekends. I've witnessed age discrimination. On multiple occasions, co-workers over 50 were laid off without warning. I assume this is a routine pruning to let go the people with the highest salaries, but it always feels kinda wrong to me. My department does regular layoffs, maybe 8-10 people get dropped every 2 years. At the same time, we're always hiring. Our use of layoffs seems like a disingenuous (disingenuous since we're hiring simultaneously) way to drop poor performers.

headline: AMS Epic Consulting
pros: Friendly and talented staff on the US teams.
cons: Deloitte's work life balance leaves much to be desired. You're expected to meet your utilization score and no matter how much they try to spin it you are punished for taking PTO. There is a lack of concern or realization of how time consuming it can be to get non client work done, which all of it is mandatory or you'll be hurt during year end reviews. To add insult most of it doesn't even apply to the AMS line, but because Deloitte is a Big 4 they expect you to learn about a bunch of irrelevant accounting and auditing topics. You can't do it during normal business hours as that will hurt your utilization. Deloitte pretends that 45 hours a week is sufficient to get Deloitte and Client work done, but you need an extra 5-15 hours on top of that number. Deloitte has a lot of documentation overhead that slow things down. I suspect we'll eventually be questioned as to why so little is getting done or why we are working so many hours. Which will lead to additional documentation to slow things down even further. Pay could be better for an Epic "consultant". Living on site is not an excuse to pay less than other Epic clients, firms, and hospitals.

headline: Perspective from a middle of the pack, both in terms of job level and employee count
pros: The people are pretty fantastic, as are the perks -- food, HR really does have innovative ways of taking care of you, transportation options. Google has been willing to open up offices where its people want to be, which has been great. There is a lot of opportunity to travel, and communicate your vision to a wider audience. I appreciate some of the hard work that has gone into building the culture and Google tries hard to maintain that. There is a sense of legacy and that great things are yet to come. This is not something that is easily sustained, yet there is so much effort here, that it just might work.
cons: Certainly it's a big company. It tries hard to not be. It tries to rekindle some of the old things that made it unique, but it seems like a lost cause for the most part. There is much less opportunity to shoot to the top. There is less and less exposure to people outside your organization and too far above your management chain. There is a lot of work to be done, and Google is pretty cheap about the way that work gets accomplished. It puts added burden on many people including engineers and lower level managers. Getting actual things accomplished and seeing how it fits into the company goals has been hard.

headline: Location means everything
pros: I would recommend this job to a friend but instill in that person that who you work with can make a world of difference! I truly enjoyed my time stateside working with a wonderful staff but would never want to experience what I did overseas again. I have worked for Serco as an ACAP (Army Career and Alumni Program) Counselor in two locations. One stateside and one overseas. The stateside experience was great. I had a wonderful supervisor and when they left another counselor was promoted to the site supervisor position. This second supervisor quickly moved up in the company and was able to work from home with a good salary. At this point I applied for the position of site supervisor aka CIM (Contract Installation Manager). I really enjoyed this experience. I was able to complete many special projects and do a lot of hiring.
cons: When I transitioned overseas I came into an ACAP office that was disorganized and did not have a supervisor on site. The CIM was located in another city and communicated via phone/email/video chat. This lead to having a "site lead", who has no authority but has many of the CIM responsibilities pushed onto them without the pay. I have a problem with a supervisor delegating work I know they are suppose to take care of without compensating the other employee. I did the job of CIM and they are taking advantage of their employees. The overseas site was also making major contract violations. They had financial counselors doing the work of career counselors, which is not in their contracts nor are they getting paid for this work. Management was timid and would avoid situations rather than confront and conquer them. The location was understaffed for the amount of clients they were expected to process. --- ACAP overhauled their program within the last two years and did a very poor job of rolling it out to its employees and clients. We were expected to present courses and complete certain tasks per contract but were give little to no resources to complete the new requiments, and I am talking basic course instruction and materials were missing. Ex "You have to start providing this new 3 hours workshop on Monday but we dont know exactly what you will be presenting on or the materials you will need". Whoever was responsible for the logistics of this contract failed big time.

headline: The people really make the place
pros: Had worked part-time in both Waitrose and John Lewis over a 4 year period and found: - pay matched with area and v. generous - pay revue every year and most employees get a generous increase (it's also based on performance not just sales targets) - great career opportunities, my manager tried to help me as much as she could with opportunities for career progression (can be difficult as are currently cutting some middle management positions). The company also has clearly set out roles so career progression can be well achieved. - benefits are great, discounts on restaurants, cinema, 25% in John Lewis, tickets to events, tickets to O2 private box - team/community atmosphere great. Amazing Christmas party in John Lewis (boat and 3 course dinner down the Thames!)
cons: - experience in Waitrose followed by John Lewis felt like two different companies. John Lewis = organised, efficient, friendly, fun, professional. Waitrose = disorganised, so unprofessional, unhelpful, rude, unknowledgeable. - had a pay dispute where they were unable to pay me for several months because I had left the firm and no one in the branch seemed to know how to add me onto payroll once I had left. Contact them on 10 different occasions and nearly went to small claims court as was having no response until it finally was resolved. They never disputed that I was owed money, they just couldn't be bothered to get round to doing it! - John Lewis dress code was quite strict, told off a few times, once for wearing a blue dress (only navy allowed) and a black and white dress that was deemed too 'patterned' even though it was one of John Lewis's own dresses from their workwear collection! Also had many compliments from customers from how nice this particular dress was, and where I got it from, so you would think they would want me to keep wearing it as I was walking free advertising! Also this strictness only seemed to apply to new employees, ones that had worked there for years seemed to get away with wearing whatever they wanted. - Something that I don't think you can avoid in retail, control over necessary actions. i.e. supposed to tell someone when you are leaving the shop floor to use the bathroom or get a drink. No water bottles on the shop floor, not allowed to leave the till for security reasons even though customers would come up to you and ask for your help, were told when you are having lunch and didn't have much choice. - Think some of the (unfortunately) male senior managers got a bit of a power trip from intimidating younger members of staff. Not sure if it is because it is retail or a sales role but thought on occasion they forgot that we were supposed to be working as a 'team'. - not much flexibility in holidays. Have to book your holidays in like September/ October for the following year. I don't know when I want to take my holiday in August in the previous October! Also once holiday was booked don't even think about asking to change as you've got no chance. If you wanted to switch days or not work a particular shift (I worked weekends so had the odd wedding/ family birthday) you had to find someone to cover your shift for you, they didn't help at all in finding someone. - management differed so much between store, John Lewis amazing, Waitrose super inefficient. Would sometimes get phone calls really last minute asking if I could work on that day even though they knew I was at college/ school and they were often very pushy and wouldn't take no for an answer. Sometimes would sign me up for shifts and the rule was if you were on the rota you were working, couldn't cross it out or say you can't do it. So manager used to sign me up to shifts, tell me I'm working and then give me no choice if I didn't want to do it! If they just timetabled better then they would have enough staff but very often they would only look at the timetable on the DAY of. It's very unreasonable to call someone at 4.30pm and expect them to come into work for 5pm and if you don't it's seen as not 'helping the business' or 'working as a team'.

headline: Run away as fast as you can
pros: -It is public accounting experience and currently the 5th largest, so that will look good on your resume' -There are social activities within the office that you have the opportunity to participate in -They pay for your CPA study material and for you to take each part (only paying for you to take it once)
cons: Where to begin: -The pay is below average. You work long hour days and the amount for which you are getting paid is less than someone working as a Dental Assistant for $15 an hour. That is when you think about the amount per hours you put in slaving. -The office politics...atrocious. Managers/Sr. Managers/Partners have favorites. That is a blessing and a curse. A blessing, because these people will speak highly of you. A curse, because now, you're the go to for everything, causing you to be over-worked and stressed out. Meanwhile, the average good performer to low performers have less work to do, and the balance is completely off. -This company lays off people at will; yet they cannot explain how they determined which individuals to get rid of. They will do this towards the end of busy season, right after you spent the last 3.5 months trying to make them happy and get the tax and audit work done. -There is no work-life balance, especially for people with families. The job comes first before your family and that is a sacrifice you are supposed to make. -They talk about the flexibility of being able to not just work in the office; however, if you work from home, they still judge you, regardless if you are actually completing your work. -It is supposed to be a team environment, but there are several instances where people get thrown under the bus...in most cases when it is not their fault. -There should be a standard procedure for each engagement...but there seems to be managers who like to have their own preferences; therefore, expect to do your work in 10 different ways to please all of these people. -One of the pros was that they pay for your CPA exam. Well, good luck studying for it while working here. -There is zero upper management transparency. You tell them issues with the firm and they do not respond with an effective solution. -HR here is a joke. The professionalism and the protocols in which they do things needs to be reevaluated ASAP. -This new "rebranding"...it's kind of failing. No one really recognizes the name RSM as much as they recognized McGladrey.

Thousands of employees with more than 25 years of service have been released since then and no longer get 6 months. So when IBM loses contracts or clients cut back on work, IBM gives those employees 1-2 months to find another IBM job and if they cannot find one (tough competition and many posting are just for show, with 'fill by' dates that keep getting pushed out), they are out the door with their 1 month of severance. It is disgraceful how low IBM has stooped to save money and treat long-time employees that helped build the company. Just google "ibm severance package".

headline: Cult of growth
pros: Competent and mostly helpful colleagues. Extreme amount of information accessible. Very powerful tools. Huge infrastructure for experimenting. Memegen.
cons: Cult of growth. Everything is measured, quantified and evaluated in terms of growth and impact. Exponential growth is expected in every single metric: number of projects, number of users, lines of code, impact, whatever. If something stops growing, it usually gets killed. Do you remember Google Reader? It stopped growing. Look out for your own stats, and get transferred quickly if you stop growing at your current place. Lack of focus. Hyperactive and very disruptive development in most areas, with user experience neglected. It is starting to hit back (as of 2014-2015). Unfortunately, I can't go into details on the consequences of this one, due to confidentiality. Chaos. There is no stable point, everything changes all the time. All documentation is unfinished and/or outdated. Very few people have the 'big picture' and they don't have time to share it, because they have to chase their own growth. Reorganization is continually happening. People come and go, teams come and go, products come and go. Usually we move 3-4 times a year. Noogler onboarding is often forgotten. There's a story about a noogler haunting the buildings for 2 months before finding out whom he reported to. I'm not sure if that ever happened, but I've seen people wandering around for several days. (Now I have the routine to spot them and help finding their team.) Long working hours and stress. This is most prevalent in SRE, but many development teams experience it, too. Cult vocabulary. There are hundreds of words for common things. On top of that, all projects have their internal codenames, and sometimes 3-4 different names refer to the same thing. You can speak whole sentences with words that only googlers understand. Willpower, Ikea, magnet, batman, etc.: those words do not mean what you think they mean. Location-specific issues. The company is centered around Mountain View, and you are almost certainly required to move there if you become important. Other sites (especially non-US sites) provide significantly less perks and choices. Mountain View is extremely crowded, and facilities can't keep up with the growth. Property prices are crazily inflated by googlers, and traffic is bad for the same reason. London still has some office space, but it pays much less than other sites, while living costs are the same or higher. The company sets the salaries based purely on industry average, not on living costs. The London benchmark seems to be flawed. You can't afford to rent any decent flat near the office, and commute is awful during peak times. Offices are open plan everywhere. Waiting for male toilets is very common at most sites. With regards to quality of life, the Zurich site is the most livable in Europe, and maybe New York in the US (until Eric Schmidt applies his stupid crowdedness-makes-you-creative theory).

headline: Gaslighting
pros: I worked with some really cool people, some really smart people.
cons: This is a severely toxic organization - reorgs and a lot of political fighting, posturing and sabotage between the VPs as they try really hard to get noticed by the EVPs. What's worse is that it appears that the HR folks are either powerless and so they go along or they are in on it. Several coworkers described experiences of being horribly berated by hatchet folks in HR based on "complaints" that HR would not clarify or explain. They described being pulled onto phone calls and told they have to "apologize for what you did", and when asked what they were talking about, would be told "it's impossible that you don't know what we're talking about and if you don't then it's even worse than we thought." Some have hypothesized this is how Salesforce rattles employees they, for whatever reason, decide they want to leave ( inside scoop indicates this is another maneuver by some VPs to create "opportunities" to shape an org the way they want when they get key folks to self-select out) but have no reason to push them out or worse yet, the employees were actually considered high performing by prior managers. I highly recommend anyone considering Salesforce to stay away unless it is the best you can get because its a huge company, if you get on the wrong side of just about anyone it could get really bad for you and there is nothing you can do.

headline: The Apple Stores are the place to be.
pros: Apple is a great place to work if you are into the latest technology. They do a really good job of showing you everything you have to know to help out customers. The company is always promoting personal growth and does their best to help you and promote you. I started working there towards the end of the summer, buy December I had been made into a part-time employee and had been given a raise. In the spring, I was given another raise because of my performance. And that was due to the fact, they kept training us and giving us lots of useful information to use out on the selling floor. I love the fact that they don't make it all about commission. It's more about helping out the customer and finding out the right solution for them. In the end, that's what retail should really be about.
cons: One of the downsides of working at Apple is that at times many people feel like they're being pressured to sell certain things. The fact is, Apple is only trying to make sure every customer gets the most out of the product. They encourage us to ask lots and lots of questions to find out what the customer's needs are. Our job is to let others know of the different services available to them. If the customer finds that service useful, then they can use it. Other employees feel like they are pushing people to buy stuff when they mention the services because they are not asking the right questions. If I know a customer has been a Mac user for a number of years, then there might be some things I leave out that wouldn't really pertain to their needs. If you make it a habit of talking to all your customers and mentioning everything, then the metrics take care of themselves. I used to think it wasn't true, but it really is. That's how I got about three raises in less than 2 years. The only other thing I don't like about Apple is the fact that starting in November (around Thanksgiving), requesting time off is strongly discouraged until after January (because of Macworld). I understand they need people to be selling and that they holidays are coming up, but we do have family and friends we like to spend time with. A weekend off during the holiday season will not hurt anybody.

headline: Different experiences
pros: - 40% off clothing and New Look Perks including discounts off cinema tickets and phones etc - 25% family and friends - Met and work with lovely people
cons: I have worked in a small and 2 large stores and the larger stores are 10x harder to work in for definate. The company have had to make cut backs and there just simply are not enough staff members to keep the shop running to its best potential. Covering manager for maternity was not suitable for the role as they did not have the best people skill set and after constantly asking for different shifts to make it fairer between the management team and to gain experience in visual merchandising and other job roles, that was not met and was told 'it's for the business's needs'. Store has gone downhill since last manager was there as she was brilliant. The last 8 months have been very challenging for this store regardless of who runs it. Sales expected to be produced with as little as two days notice, promotions always being added because the company cannot sell the product as none of the customers want it. Hours always changing and short notice for everything the company want to add on a DAILY basis is rediculous and staff are getting seriously fed up working for a company that cannot make up their minds on which day they want a particular project to launch when the company expect you have full flexibility for a 4/8/16 hour contract. No loyalty from the company or some managers, can go in and never have a day sick, always come in early, work 6 or 7 days a week, never complain and never even get a thank you. Training can't even be thought about for people who want to progress in the company as the payroll just isn't there and positions are being closed down to save costs, so it's harder to progress in the business. Customers are becoming more and more demanding every year making your job harder (not made easier by New Look with the approach the have towards customers). Sounds like a mostly negative experience, but have been enjoying working more recently since moving to a smaller store as it's less work loads on less people and an amazing store manager. Would love to be able to speak to big bosses to give them an insight into how I/we feel!

headline: Long hours, random schedule, just another retail store
pros: Great benefits from day one. Co-workers are generally nice and pretty enthusiastic.
cons: Despite all the talk about "positioning" and "expectations" in the interview process, it all seems lost in the store environment. The CORE training says Apple encourages feedback across management lines, but in practice it seems like feedback in all downstream. The mantra is "this is retail" which is at least a shot at honesty. Training time for creatives is not a priority even though pro certifications are high on the priority list. So I guess I expected to get the opportunity to learn more in-depth stuff about Apple pro software and then teach it to customers who are using those products. Instead creatives at our store are used as fill ins anywhere else in the store when we are not training. There is also some subtle sexism from management, including the women (most of whom seems to be from some other mall store management position), and they don't approach me with technical or software questions the way they do my male co-workers. Work/life balance is not on anyone's balance sheet either, so expect to make attempts to rearrange your life around a totally random schedule. No matter how hard you work, you have to self motivate, at least at this store, because that is the only motivation you will get. I am really disappointed this has turned out like this and am using my few days off, and I mean that literally, we often work eight in a row, to look for more reasonable work (even in this tough economy). My work ethic is huge, and I will continue to work as hard as I can to make the customers in my store happy and make them feel valued until I move on.

headline: IBM Research is a unique place
pros: At IBM Research you are surrounded by a lot of very smart people and many innovative projects. People are highly focused on their research topics and there is a lot of diversity among co-workers. New ideas are encouraged and there is funding for "adventurous" research projects as well as short-term projects which contribute directly to software group products. People are encouraged to participate in the academic community by collaborating with professors, and publishing papers in conferences and journals. Generating IP in terms of patents is also rewarded.
cons: IBM Research is not well connected to IBM's customers. We always have to go through another layer or 2 of IBM sales or services to deliver anything to the customer. The other divisions of IBM have incentives and motives that are not always aligned with Research's success. Though some projects are funded by IBM itself, departments have goals for the revenue they need to bring in from outside IBM and the bureaucracy and layering makes it difficult to reach those goals. Also, within IBM Research there are Research Staff Members (typically PhDs) and Software Engineers (more likely MS holders) and the projects are usually focused around the interests of the RSMs, with SW Engrs in basically supporting roles.

headline: Average but improving

I’m on the consulting side called Global Business Solutions, rather than the more famous innovation side called Global Technical Solutions. As a consulting firm, they are about average. They seem to have discovered--and are taking seriously--customer satisfaction.
cons: It is very difficult to find resources. The benefits are continually reducing. For example, they no long match 401(k) contributions with each paycheck. They wait to see if you're still around at the end of the year and make a lump sum payment so they, not you, get the benefits of dollar-cost averaging. People management is an extra duty assigned to someone who is being rewarded for doing something else. Getting a helpful manager is luck-of the-draw (and the odds are no in your favor). Finding your next assignment or developing your skills is entirely up to you.

headline: IBM GSDC Poland Wrocław (CIC Wrocław & Katowice) a great place to work with great group of people
pros: 1. Extremely dedicated HR team, in my 10+ years of work experience working with various multinational companies, I have never seen a more dedicated and friendly HR team as I came to know one exists in IBM CIC Wrocław. They were always available for assistance throughout the year long process and through very difficult times of COVID crisis. (really exceptional job). 2. Amazing team of technical staff, (this obviously depends on the team that a person joins in to), as far as I can say my team was very welcoming and extremely supportive. They provided all possible help to me and brought me up to speed on anything that was required to work and provide great delivery to the customer. 3. Great manager (this is again going to vary from person to person) but as far as my manager is concerned, he is the most level minded person and an exceptional character, he literally makes all possible efforts to make the team work to the best of their abilities, I have never come across a manager with such exceptional capabilities. He a real gem in this IT world where you can really have terrifying experiences with your managers (which is more likely to happen). 4. An infinite learning opportunity. Literally the biggest benefit of working at IBM is the immensely massive source of learning. And now thanks to IBM's partnership with udemy the massively large source has become even more mega. 5. Work life balance, for all those people who are looking for balancing their work and personal life. It is really a great place that affords you all that liberty.
cons: 1. Uncertainty of company structure due to new announcement of "NewCo" spin off. 2. Lots of possible lay-offs and cost cutting (this is not new IBM has always found ways to do that). 3. Bureaucratic management structure , takes time to process anything , hence things move slowly which can be frustrating at times. (But hopefully that may change if one thing is to improve with "NewCo" spin off) 4. Salaries are not competitive compared to rest of the market players, (IBMers are never happy with their salary compensation and hikes but that has always been the fact historically, people work here not for the money , but for the joy of the technology and for the learning and growth).

headline: It ALL depends on your manager
pros: 1. With the right manager, you have access to potentially life-changing career advancement opportunities 2. In some groups, you have the chance to work with people who are the best in the industry 3. If you've got a family and want free insurance coverage for the whole brood, MS is the place for you 4. Casual-dress culture and the tradition that still endures of periodic "morale events" for teams is nice 5. If you're in the right position in the right group, you can get exposure to Microsoft business expertise (even if you're in a technical discipline) that will stand you in great stead in the future
cons: 1. With the wrong manager, there's nothing you can do to succeed 2. If your project goes into crunch mode for the longterm, you could find yourself stuck with 80 hour weeks and no alternative other than to do them or leave the company, because there are ways to hold you on your team if they don't want to let you leave (related to: wrong manager) 3. No raises without a promo, I hear, currently 4. Jobs can be so narrow, and involve so much administrative overhead, that you spend a lot of your time on work that doesn't enhance your skill set or make you more employable elsewhere in the future 5. The company's spending money on what seem to be money-sinks right now, which is good if you want to get into a money-sink team with a fancy title and leave it in a couple years for another company, but not necessarily good for the long term 6. Don't say you were not warned: the same job can be titled and compensated very differently depending on the organization. In general, money-sink groups like search and Xbox tend to offer better compensation than bread-and-butter established groups like servers, Windows client, and Office. 7. Even if you carefully select a team to join based on its manager, which is the recommended way to do it at MS (choose manager first, then job), this can get up-ended by a divisional or departmental reorganization that can give you a manager that is not a good fit for you and there's not much you can do about it

headline: Better than most places. Still tons of hours and travel.
pros: Good salary and benefits (not great, considering the hours and travel). Looks great on a resume and very good experience, but the business consulting (non-internal audit) is a recent practice that they've been rebuilding since about 2008. It's had a rapid growth and those joining now missed the bottom floor entry, but also many growing pains (like a huge lack of practice resources, tools, knowledge databases, etc.). Still small in comparison to Deloitte, Accenture, but closing the gap.
cons: Way more of an old boys club feel than other Big 4 firms. Few women in business consulting (read: not tax or internal audit) above level of manager. EY is not anti-women and the women that are there are outstanding and very pro-women. It's just that the guys tend to go to lunch together and hang out together outside of work (not just at the associate/senior levels) so if you're not "one of the guys" it can be tough to build the strong relationships needed to get pulled in to sell work or be assigned to work on good projects. This may be a result of so many sr managers & partners returning to EY from Cap Gemini (EY consulting that was spun off in the late 90's) once their non-compete agreement w/EY expired. From my experience and conversations with friends, KPMG and Deloitte seem more pro-female. Performance Improvement managers must average 45 hrs a week billable to be at 100% utilzation, but many clients only allow you to bill 40 hrs, so if this gives you very litle room during the year if you are between engagement. Lots of people get hurt by this, especailly, if a client pushes back a start date and you're the subject matter resource for the project (and can't quickly be deployed elsewhere).

headline: Manager - Deloitte Consulting
pros: - Great resume builder; other recruiters and companies positively respond to the Deloitte brand (and to management consulting in general) - Good empowerment in managing one's own career; you can work in any industry / function as long as you yourself make the effort to make it happen (i.e., network with leadership, contribute free time to project proposals, etc.) - Generally collegial coworkers, especially at the more junior levels - Interesting project work that takes you across different business problems and industries - Strong management team that is steering the company is the right direction (from a strategic point of view); good job security - Points / airline miles from travel and dining out - Expense accounts are generally lenient (but depend on the client / project) - Good health benefits - Pension plan that vests after three years
cons: - Unrelenting demands. Asking for free time to yourself is generally frowned upon. headline: Barratt Apprenticeships
pros: Employee Benefits: Barratts offer a range of employee benefits which make them a very desirable company to work for. For example; their share save scheme in which you can buy shares for a set price of £4.20 (when I entered the scheme) which is reasonably lower than buying them anywhere else, and if their shares drop below this number you get the full amount you paid in back, ensuring you don't lose any money. This alongside other benefits like childcare, holiday buybacks and we were also offered 200 shares twice whilst I have been working for them which equates to over £2000. They pay me very well as an apprentice which is surprising as I have experienced and witnessed some apprentices earn next to nothing and get abused by their employers. There is opportunity for career progression with Barratts, they like to promote their staff internally and will invest in you to do specialist training and degrees in the field you will work in. They are a generous employer also, they often give performance based bonuses at Christmas and the site managers receive bonuses for winning NHBC awards. I was also rewarded with a bonus for winning Apprentice of the year.
cons: If you are looking into going to work for Barratts I would say go for it as they are a very fair and supportive company to work for. I would think twice however if you are thinking of becoming an apprentice to learn a trade. All apprentices should be working with the trades to learn their trade, for the majority of the three years I spent working for them I did not, and as the recession approaches from the pandemic they have done me no favours. They offered me a job to continue working for them indefinitely, however because of the pandemic this is no longer possible, and because their apprenticeship programme is flawed and I spent the majority of my time at Barratts not learning a proper trade I found myself unprepared to go and work as a carpenter despite being fully qualified. However this is the fault of my individual site manager and contracts manager and does not reflect the company as whole. If you are looking to become an apprentice for a large home builder I know that Taylor Wimpey are a far better option.

headline: Was once good, but go elsewhere if you want respect.
pros: - RSM as a whole is a great firm that truly knows what it wants to deliver to its clients - Depending on the industry you choose to work in, you will get to travel to many places around the U.S. - Firm covers lots of lunches at restaurants, happy hours, other celebrations - If you travel, you quickly accumulate tons of travel rewards points - If you're still working on your CPA exam, they cover the cost of review materials and the fees to take each section (they pay for each section one time) - There's a chance you might work with really cool and interesting clients - Lots of great exposure to different industries and individuals - Great access to CEOs, CFOs, upper management of companies that you don't get elsewhere when you're just coming out of college
cons: - If you travel a lot, they used to have a great travel bonus program but they took that away, so for those who are stuck traveling 4-5 months out of the year, you have no incentives or perks, just a loss of any type of life outside of work. - The office constantly states they encourage a work-life balance but you are shunned if you so much as make an attempt to have a life outside of work - Many Managers and Partners tell you to always ask questions but once you do, they are openly annoyed and tell you to figure it out yourself/tell you they're busy/ignore you. - Managers and Partners don't care about staff, they give absolutely NO support and don't train or teach their staff at all and then get mad when staff asks a question or work is wrong (work would be better if they taught staff) - In-Charges (seniors) try to help but they have so much pressure on them they can't take the time to teach as much as they want to - Senior management and other areas of employees will drink with new staff in an unprofessional way. - Associates who suck up to the managers and partners are treated much better than associates who do their work and act professional - LOTS of gossip about fellow employees throughout the office. People will be nice to your face and act like they like you and want to help you, and then rip you apart in meetings/reviews. Managers and Partners also make fun of the students they meet during campus recruiting. - Lots of inappropriate behavior and treatment occurs, but nothing is ever done about it even if Managers/Partners/HR are told. HR does nothing to help. - They always press that they want you to move up in your career but do nothing to help you get there. They will assign you difficult audits/projects, give you no assistance, and then bash you when it's not done fast enough - TONS of favoritism - Compensation is subpar compared to other firms of the same size. - Managers pay no attention to their clients, they only care about the ones that have the highest fees, leaving Seniors to constantly come up with reasons to tell the client why their work isn't getting finished. - No support from upper management results in lower audit quality - Completely unrealistic budgets coupled with not enough resources Management needs to open their eyes and pay attention to what is happening in their office. Issues start at the top and fall downwards. This office will keep deteriorating until a significant change occurs and Staff is appreciated for their efforts, respected, supported, and gossiping and favoritism is eliminated. All of the focus is on the bottom line of the audits, which will be bad until staff/seniors are properly taught by their superiors. There's no consistency among the audits and no real training on how the firm wants work to be completed from start to finish. The "unity" and "encouragement" in the office is laughable.

cons: There is very little planned leadership or accountability. Crisis Management seems to rule the day. If someones continually screws up as an employee or a manager, no one takes the time to address the issue or fix the problem. A very ethically-challenged organization. You are required to take ethics training every 2 years, and you just look around and see all of the violations. Some are downright criminal. But what do you do when Larry himself has a enormous conflict of interest (see NetSuite)? I also don't trust the anonymity of the tool used to report violations. The company loves to offshore and use H1-B workers. The problem here is they seem to hire very incompetent people. Your job will be to put out fires that they create. Middle Management knows whats going on, but has no authority to do anything. Whether it is rewarding job performance, hiring or firing people, everything is run from the top. This means you get the same bonus at the guy who shows up to work 3 days a week. This also makes it very undesirable to pursue a career here.

headline: The worst move I ever made
pros: The only benefit is the ability to work from home although the company demands you to go into the office a couple of times a week.
cons: The pressure from the offset is immense and try and imagine your busiest day and then multiple that by 4 (for each of your clients); 1 (for holiday cover) and then to top it off you’ll have an annual appraisal every 6 weeks. They use an NPS system (no, I’d never heard of it either) and you must get 9-10 out of 10. If you don’t achieve these scores you’re put on a Performance Improvement Plan and shown the door. You’re judged by your colleagues, clients and the inexperienced management team. There are no processes in place and no-one to turn to. You’ll also be expected to upsell your hours. So if you think you don’t have any more time, well think again. The management team want you to increase your hours so they get more money. You’ll never be able to add any value to each client as you’re fire fighting every single minute of every day. This is factory work dressed up as an EA role. You’ll also need to provide your own laptop and mobile phone. There are no benefits whatsoever. The turnover is very high. Once EAs realise they’ve been mis-sold they leave very quickly. This isn't a happy place to work. Steer well clear of this company and don’t be fooled into thinking you’ll be able to do your regular EA job from home. Very far from it. It is the most stressful and unpleasant job I’ve ever had and can’t strongly enough advise people to give it a wide berth. My NPS score to the management team is nil point.

headline: Reinventing retail? Not for the employees.
pros: Many of your co-workers will be intelligent, funny people who are a real pleasure to work with and to get to know. You'll be able to tell everyone you know that you work for Apple, which carries a certain respect with it. Your healthcare benefits package will be excellent. You'll never have to use a PC at work.
cons: First of all, despite what you're told at hiring events and new employee training, you don't really work for Apple, Inc. Instead, you work for Apple Retail, which is for all intents and purposes an entirely different company. There is little to no career connection between the two, and retail employees are looked upon as second class citizens by corporate employees. Your chances of getting promoted from Apple Retail to Apple Corporate are no better than they would be if you worked for anywhere else. In fact, they might be worse. The day to day routine of working for Apple Retail has some significant problems. You can expect that your needs will always come second to "the needs of the business." In fact, anytime you hear that phrase, be prepared for the next sentence to describe how you're going to be screwed. For example, "I'm sorry, Joe, but the needs of the business dictate that you can't take a vacation between October and February, or June through September" or "Well, the needs of the business mean we can't give you a fixed schedule." Your schedule will be erratic. You may work from 2 PM to 12 AM on Tuesday and be expected to come in at 8 AM the following day. If there's a product being launched (iPhone, iPad, etc), you may be asked to work overnight to set up the store, then come back in the next day and work another shift. Sometimes you're asked to work straight through. During normal weeks your shifts will often be right in the middle of the day, leaving you little time to accomplish anything before or after. No scheduling preference is given based on seniority, family considerations, or any other factor. Any and all time off must be requested in writing, often several months in advance, but your schedule won't arrive until a few days before it goes into effect. Long stretches of the year are blacked out for vacation time, due to the needs of the business. Favored employees will often be given a pass to take vacations during this time, especially senior managers. Your coworkers will be neatly divided into two groups: those who are able to rationalize any decision made by Apple Inc, and those who understand the company for what it really is. There will be many more of the former than the latter. If you're a member of the relentlessly optimistic tribe, you can probably do very well in Apple Retail. If you're not, be prepared to hear impromptu speeches about how Apple products "change" and "enrich" people's lives, and how amazing it is to work at Apple. Many of these people will be older, and some will have either failed at or quit other careers to sell computers for a few dollars above minimum wage, which adds an undertone of desperation to their happy message. If you find yourself in the less optimistic camp, be prepared to be part of a very small minority, and get ready to hear about it when you decide to speak your mind. In fact, don't speak your mind. Overall, Apple Retail is a place that spends a lot of time and money to promote the idea that they Really Care about their employees. One of the first things you're given when you're hired is the Credo Card, which lays out all that Apple Retail stands for and believes in. The very first line of the card is, "At Apple our heart and soul is our people." But what you'll come to realize over time is that Apple Retail doesn't care about you at all. They care about making money, and above all pleasing the customers. And that's it. If you hope to have a long, successful and rewarding career at Apple Retail, you'd better really love retail for it's own sake. Loving the products isn't enough, in time you'll grow to resent them. You need to love all the complicated, illogical, arcane intricacies that make up the American retail model. If you do, you'll probably do very well at Apple. If not, it won't be long before you'll be looking for a way out.

headline: Great for a little while
pros: It's very laid back and great atmosphere. Possibility to make good money. Restaurant is located by the main pools. It's outdoor but covered and has flaps to close during rainy or cold weather. The employees are very nice and laid back for the most part. The travel program and room discounts are amazing if you travel often. The bussers are really good about helping with whatever you need. They have department outings once a year, they pull employees from other resorts to cover and vice versa.
cons: It's outdoor which means no AC or heat and no way to stop bugs. Always spiders in the rafters and ants in the server station. The kitchen is inconsistent with food preparation and presentation. Food is served differently depending on the cook. They are stuck in their ways for the most part. Management is afraid to make waves for the long time servers so they get away with a lot more than they should which causes newer servers to leave. Management makes rules but there's no consequences when people break them. It's outdoor so there's usually no host which means tables sit where they want unless another server grabs them first to sit them in their station. This means there is no fair rotation which leads to resentment among co-workers. There's not a nearby breakroom and since there's no host this means nowhere to take a quick break from the heat, you have to constantly be on floor greeting tables when they walk in.

headline: Below average Big 4
pros: The benefits, management training, and opportunities to work on unique projects for a wide variety of companies are obviously the biggest draw to any Big 4 company. Nothing is different at EY.
cons: In many ways, they seem to be followers in the industry. When I arrived at EY in 2014, they were still operating on Lotus Notes and were miles apart from other companies in their IT capabilities (I came from Deloitte and can verify that firsthand). For example, share point sites for collaboration and teaming were not existent. Every office was using their own templates. No one coordinated with each other. It has since gotten better but only because they had to if they didn't want to be left behind the competition. Even when it comes to benefits they provide, they follow the other Big 4. They never lead. With the recent layoffs of Senior Managers across the US in all departments, the firm is providing several months of paid employment with EY to find new employment, which is fantastic. However, it is disappointing that the effected Senior Manager group was not provided more clarity and guidance. If the message is that this group could not get to the next level due to the forecasted growth (or lack thereof) of the practice, then why not have an open conversation with these Senior Managers a year ago and speak honestly with them to give them a chance to develop into better business development personnel and sales people. Or to allow them better mentoring and coaching to develop that skillset so they can help the practice grow and allow them an opportunity to become Partners. My experience is that most of these people were 4-6 years into being Senior Managers. The firm obviously invested a lot of time and money into developing these young leaders - why not give them a kick in the butt that they maybe needed to grow into the leaders you want, rather than just pulling the plug?? Disappointing on many levels.

headline: Enjoyable
pros: I did have my reservations about joining given the fact that they are always looking for drivers, however I really do enjoy the challenges and variety this job brings. Doing store deliveries is hard work at times when you have a manual pump truck to take off the load, however this is balanced out when you have stores where you just open the curtains and let the FLT Driver get on with it. Most of the staff at the stores are great to work with, all you need to do is be friendly and helpful which makes their day. The depot colleagues and drivers are also great to work with, most are friendly. I enjoy it here, and having new Scanias to drive makes the job better! Despite it being hard work, the job is secure which is important to me.

headline: Great Culture (for Some), Good Work, but Needs Work

The focus on volunteering and giving back is incredibly important and is so appreciated. You are welcomed to be yourself, to feel comfortable in your own skin and that's a huge departure from many of the places I've been.
cons: Although there's quite a bit of discussion about family, it's something that's I have not yet experienced outside my own team. Granted I work in a regional office and not in San Francisco. I've been told there's a big difference in terms of experience when you do work at or near HQ. The regional office I work from isn't very diverse at all despite there being a stated global commitment to diversity. There seem to be four categories; sales "bros", product engineers, support, customer success. Silos are very evident between Salesforce core and recent Salesforce acquisitions. Processes are usually disjointed and there's a very significant learning curve between acquisitions and Salesforce core. Overall organizations seem a bit scattered and initiatives lack a cohesive direction in the Success organization. However, the products are strong and since sales are expanding, this definitely covers much of the inefficiencies with Support. Most notably, however, customer management seems to not seek real partnered solutions, rather it's a "do whatever the customer wants" which mean customer can be based on unfulfilled promises and misrepresented features/value without real-world expectations.

headline: They try really hard to camouflage the negatives of working here.
pros: They offer adequate compensation, and have very nice benefits including quarterly bonuses. After one year of employment, there are a lot opportunities for advancement.
cons: They promise you a schedule in the phone interview, and then give you something totally different once you're in training. They are not flexible at all when it comes to the schedule. The training program is 5 weeks long, but it doesn't mean much as they change the system so often. There was a major change in the system the day after we were trained on it, and all they said was, "Get used to change." There is nothing special about you at Booking.com. No matter how hard you work, or how high your CSAT (customer satisfaction) is, you are completely replaceable. The most you get for excelling in CSAT is a pat on the back, and a $25 gift card once in a great while. Your employment is solely dependent on your CSAT score. This is determined by a survey sent to customers via email after contact with you. More often than not, your dissatisfied surveys are due to the situation, and not your service, but there is no way to dispute this. Even if the guest leaves a comment that praises the you highly, but clicks dissatisfied by mistake, it still counts as a negative score. They constantly promote team effort, and reiterate how important it is to work with your team, but there are no opportunities to do so. Every score that affects you directly is individual, and the overall team score only affects your team leader's bonus. The senior line is the line that you call when you need help in a situation, or a customer requests to speak to the manager. We are constantly told that we call them too much, and that we need to look at the procedure guidelines before calling, but I sat next to them, and I watch them goof off, and watch Youtube videos all day. Finally, the team leads. I'm sure not all of them are as bad as mine, but mine was ridiculous. She tells us to call her when we need help, but she is never at her desk. In the one on one feedback sessions, there was no feedback, just the same goal reiterated. Before our quarterly review, she asked that we tell her what we think our strengths and weaknesses are. On my review, she copied and pasted my email to her. Literally made me review myself, and added nothing to it.

headline: 50/50 split between the good and bad points about working as a software engineer for Accenture.
pros: No blame culture - Nobody points a finger at you. I was never "told off" during my time at the company. If something goes wrong, everybody just pitches in and helps out till it's fixed. Social - Lots of nice people, always something to take part in, great if you're single. Build your own reputation - On your first day, if you dive right in head first you will get recognised and rewarded but you will be expected to keep up that level of hard-work. If you prefer a bit more balance, you can have that, and the expectations will drop, but the rewards won't be as forthcoming either. Networks - Support networks are great and something I highly compliment but a little confusing. Between your buddy, HR Rep, career councillor, line manager, etc, it's hard to know who to speak to sometimes.
cons: Terrible rewards - The pay for a software engineer is about £2-3k less than what I consider a "good" salary. The overtime system is awful, you get "half-pay" for any hours of overtime. Not time-and-a-half, but half-time. And the first 37.5 hours of that get added on to your holiday which most consider a negative. Promotions - The promotions system is awful, pretty much coming down to how much your manager likes you at a single point during the year. Flexible working - Never happens. If you have children, you can work flexibly, otherwise, you do whatever hours you're told to do. Working hours - 10 hour days were common. Longest day I think I did was about 15 hours. Usually you get the next day off after a long stint like that but having software engineers working all hours of the day... there gets a point where your productivity just drops to nothing but the management never seemed to notice; so long as you're there. Offshoring - I'd estimate that around 60-80% of the code developed offshore was of such poor quality that it needed to be overhauled/redone onshore before being deployed. Work, work, work.... - A final note. I consider myself to be a hard working individual, but Accenture takes it to a whole new level. You pretty much have to dedicate yourself to the company/project and, if you don't, there will always be somebody who will, and they'll get a promotion, and you won't, despite the fact your quality of work is twice as good.

headline: A disorganised, political mess with fundamental failings
pros: There are people in this business who want to do a good job, and want to succeed
cons: Micromanagement is prevalent The focus on task is so intense, that many managers within the business have lost sight of what that task is intended to achieve, and thus any deviation in the search for better ways of working is a frightening concept for them Planning is almost non-existent. It is a rarity for colleagues to have more than a week’s schedule in advance. Despite a company rule stating no colleague’s shifts to be amended with less than 48hours notice without consent, this happens on a daily basis. This has included new starters having no schedule until 4 days after their induction, a colleague getting their first week’s schedule after the end of their second shift that week, and colleagues returning from annual leave to find their days and times of work completely changed. Employee welfare concern is non-existent. Return to work meetings are a rarity, and the outcomes of those meetings are ignored with colleagues asked to work beyond what has been agreed as reasonable amendments. Managers are encouraged to spend hours watching colleagues working on CCTV to observe what is being done, acting in hindsight rather than work alongside and lead their teams. The management structure and culture within the company is task oriented with an attitude geared towards breaking down colleagues for fault and blame. The inability of key managers to build and develop teams and individuals is crippling and resulting in excessive employee turnover.

headline: Want to be on the front line of the technology world - then it is a place for you, but be aware of what to expect
pros: Very dynamic and very innovative company with a lot of opportunities to grow and develop yourself. A lot of nice and well educated people of different art and personalities. Company supports people development as well as the people themselves. Be ready to be dynamic person and flexible as company moves very fast and changes internally also fast. Be ready for continues learning and self development - company gives you a lot of opportunities to learn, and expects you to grow continuously. Company gives a lot of flexibility in term of your time - flexible working time, flexible hours and even location. The main focus is on the tasks assigned to you being completed. This means - be sure you commit to what is possible to deliver, otherwise it might lead to overtime, which in most cases is not compensated. Be aware: this is a big international company - networking is a key for the career development, and for the daily business. A lot of things are happening in the same time - hence you will be in the situation when something happens and you are not aware of it - keep networking to be simply up to date. In some cases even relocation to other countries and regions is possible. if you young, talented and get to the high potential pool - you might get into the job rotation mode (very selected group of employees). Be ready to move and grow within the company, if you are about to make a management career - be active in this regards. All in all - a nice place to work.
